title: Why humanoid robots matter to China
description:
Videos from the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing have been going viral. Two thousand robots from 16 countries took part and the robots seem more human-like than ever. They dance, compete in boxing matches, sprint faster than Usain Bolt, and even lift weights (not always successfully).

BBC China Analyst Kerry Allen explains how the Games relate to China’s international and domestic goals. Among other things, China’s leaders want to show the world how advanced their robotics industry is and demonstrate advances that will allow robots to strengthen China’s workforce.

We also hear reactions from content creators Christina Ernst in the United States, Uchechukwu Ololo in Nigeria and Cheryl Liu in China.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討中國在北京舉行的世界人形機器人大賽及其背後的戰略意圖與影響。賽事中人形機器人展現了跑步、舞蹈甚至以 9.39 秒超越 Usain Bolt 紀錄的 100 公尺衝刺等技能，但也出現摔倒與失火等故障情形。BBC 中國媒體分析師 Kerry Allen 指出，在國際上，中國希望展示其領先的技術實力並協助開發中國家；在國內，受過去獨生子女政策引發的人口減少與老化影響，中國迫切需要機器人填補勞動力缺口。儘管網路內容創作者 Uchechukwu Ololo 與 Cheryl Liu 等人對取代人類工作表達疑慮，中國政府強調將實施人類監督，並透過機器人產業創造全新的就業機會。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World examines the viral World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing and China's strategic motivations behind advancing its robotics industry. BBC China analyst Kerry Allen explains that internationally, China aims to showcase its technological leadership over competitors like the US and assist developing nations. Domestically, humanoid robots are key to addressing labor shortages driven by an aging and shrinking population stemming from the former one-child policy. While content creators express concerns over job displacement, Allen notes that the Chinese government emphasizes human oversight and expects the expanding robotics sector to create new employment opportunities.
